questions.stem: What is an anabolic reaction?
options: A reaction that moves molecules across a membrane against their gradient
A reaction that takes place only outside cells, in the digestive tract
A reaction that builds larger molecules from smaller ones and uses energy
A reaction that breaks larger molecules into smaller ones and releases energy
questions.explanation: Anabolic reactions synthesise complex molecules, such as proteins from amino acids, and need an input of energy. Breaking molecules down and releasing energy is catabolism.

questions.stem: Which of these is a catabolic reaction?
options: Fatty acids and glycerol being joined to form a triglyceride
Glycogen being broken down into glucose in a liver cell
Amino acids being joined to form a protein at a ribosome
Glucose molecules being joined to form glycogen in muscle
questions.explanation: Catabolism breaks large molecules into smaller ones, as when glycogen is broken down to glucose. The other three are all syntheses, so they are anabolic.

questions.stem: How do enzymes speed up metabolic reactions in cells?
options: By lowering the activation energy needed for the reaction to proceed
By supplying the energy that the reaction needs in the form of ATP
By raising the temperature of the cell so molecules collide more often
By becoming part of the product so that less reactant is needed
questions.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts that lower the activation energy, so reactions run quickly at body temperature. They are not used up or built into the products.

questions.stem: Salivary amylase digests starch but has no effect on protein. What explains this specificity?
options: It is made in only one organ, so it only ever meets one substrate
It is destroyed after catalysing a single reaction
It can only work at one exact temperature and pH
Its active site has a shape that fits only a particular substrate
questions.explanation: An enzyme's specificity comes from the shape and chemistry of its active site, which binds only substrates of complementary shape. Enzymes are reused many times, not destroyed.

questions.stem: How does the induced fit model differ from the lock and key model of enzyme action?
options: The active site is rigid and exactly matches the substrate before binding
The active site changes shape slightly to fit closely around the substrate
The substrate changes shape permanently before it ever reaches the active site
The enzyme binds to any substrate and then selects the correct product
questions.explanation: In the induced fit model the active site is flexible and moulds around the substrate as it binds, stressing bonds. A rigid, exactly matching site is the older lock and key idea.

questions.stem: What happens to an enzyme that is heated well above its optimum temperature?
options: It becomes inactive but recovers its full activity as soon as it is cooled
It changes into a different enzyme that catalyses a different type of reaction
It denatures: its active site changes shape and no longer binds the substrate
It works faster indefinitely because its molecules have more kinetic energy
questions.explanation: High temperature breaks the weak bonds holding the enzyme's three-dimensional shape, altering the active site permanently. Low temperature, by contrast, only slows an enzyme, and activity returns on warming.

questions.stem: Pepsin works in the stomach and trypsin works in the small intestine. Which pair of optimum pH values is most likely?
options: Pepsin about pH 7; trypsin about pH 7
Pepsin about pH 5; trypsin about pH 11
Pepsin about pH 2; trypsin about pH 8
Pepsin about pH 8; trypsin about pH 2
questions.explanation: The stomach is strongly acidic because of hydrochloric acid, while pancreatic juice makes the small intestine slightly alkaline. Each enzyme's optimum suits where it works.

questions.stem: An enzyme's activity is measured at 5 °C, cooled samples are then warmed to 37 °C, and others are heated to 70 °C and then cooled to 37 °C. Which result is expected at 37 °C?
options: Both sets of samples show the same activity once returned to 37 °C
The cooled-then-warmed samples are active; the heated samples are not
The heated samples are active; the cooled-then-warmed samples are not
Neither set of samples shows any activity once returned to 37 °C
questions.explanation: Cold only slows enzymes by reducing collisions, so activity returns on warming. Heating to 70 °C denatures a human enzyme, and the change in shape is not reversed by cooling.

questions.stem: A competitive inhibitor slows an enzyme-catalysed reaction. How does it work?
options: It reacts with the substrate so the substrate can no longer bind
It raises the temperature so that the enzyme slowly denatures
It binds to the active site, blocking the substrate from entering
It binds to a different site and permanently changes the active site
questions.explanation: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and occupies the active site. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere on the enzyme and changes the active site's shape.

questions.stem: Adding much more substrate overcomes the effect of inhibitor X but not of inhibitor Y. What does this suggest?
options: Both X and Y are competitive inhibitors
Both X and Y are non-competitive inhibitors
X is competitive and Y is non-competitive
X is non-competitive and Y is competitive
questions.explanation: Extra substrate outcompetes a competitive inhibitor for the active site. A non-competitive inhibitor changes the active site wherever it binds, so more substrate cannot restore the rate.

questions.stem: What is a co-enzyme?
options: A protein that blocks the active site to stop an enzyme working too quickly
An organic non-protein molecule, often made from a vitamin, that helps an enzyme work
An inorganic ion, such as zinc or magnesium, that must bind to an enzyme to activate it
A second enzyme that breaks down the products of the first enzyme's reaction
questions.explanation: Co-enzymes are organic molecules, many derived from B group vitamins, that carry atoms or electrons between reactions. Inorganic ions that assist enzymes are called co-factors.

questions.stem: Some enzymes work only when a metal ion such as magnesium or zinc is attached. What is this ion called?
options: A co-enzyme
A substrate
An inhibitor
A co-factor
questions.explanation: An inorganic ion needed for enzyme activity is a co-factor. Co-enzymes are organic molecules, such as those made from vitamins.

questions.stem: Why can a diet lacking certain B group vitamins slow cellular respiration?
options: These vitamins form the active sites of the enzymes in the mitochondria
Without these vitamins oxygen cannot diffuse into cells from the blood
Co-enzymes needed by respiratory enzymes are made from these vitamins
These vitamins are the main fuel broken down to release energy in cells
questions.explanation: Several co-enzymes that carry hydrogen and electrons in respiration are made from B vitamins, so a shortage limits the enzymes that depend on them. Vitamins are not a fuel source.

questions.stem: Enzyme concentration is kept constant while substrate concentration is increased. The rate rises and then levels off. Why does it level off?
options: The product has run out, so the reaction can no longer continue
The substrate has begun to inhibit the enzyme competitively
All the active sites are occupied, so the enzyme is working at its maximum rate
The enzyme has been denatured by the high concentration of substrate
questions.explanation: Once every active site is in use at any instant, adding substrate cannot increase the rate; enzyme concentration has become the limiting factor. The enzyme is not denatured.

questions.stem: In a metabolic pathway, the final product inhibits the enzyme that catalyses the first step. What is the effect of this arrangement?
options: When the product builds up the pathway speeds up, so more product is made
The first enzyme is denatured, so the pathway stops permanently
The product is converted back into the first substrate of the pathway
When the product builds up the pathway slows, so the product is not overproduced
questions.explanation: This is end-product inhibition: a high product concentration slows the first enzyme, and as the product is used up the pathway speeds up again. It shows how product concentration controls enzyme activity.

questions.stem: Which change would increase the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction that is limited by the amount of enzyme present?
options: Lowering the temperature
Adding a competitive inhibitor
Adding more enzyme
Adding more substrate
questions.explanation: If enzyme is limiting, every active site is already busy, so only more enzyme raises the rate. Adding more substrate has no effect once the active sites are saturated.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of cellular respiration?
options: To release energy from organic compounds and store it in ATP
To exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide between the lungs and blood
To build glucose from carbon dioxide and water using energy
To break large food molecules into small ones in the gut
questions.explanation: Cellular respiration is the catabolism of organic molecules such as glucose inside cells to make ATP. Gas exchange in the lungs is sometimes loosely called respiration, but it is a different process.

questions.stem: Where in the cell does glycolysis take place?
options: In the cytosol
In the mitochondrial matrix
On the inner mitochondrial membrane
In the nucleus
questions.explanation: Glycolysis, the first stage of respiration, splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules in the cytosol. The Krebs cycle happens in the mitochondrial matrix.

questions.stem: Which word equation summarises aerobic respiration?
options: carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen + energy (ATP)
glucose -> lactic acid + carbon dioxide + energy (ATP)
glucose + carbon dioxide -> oxygen + water + energy (ATP)
glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP)
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration oxidises glucose completely to carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy that is partly stored in ATP. The reverse equation describes photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Where are the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain located?
options: Krebs cycle in the cytosol; electron transport chain on the outer mitochondrial membrane
Krebs cycle in the cytosol; electron transport chain in the mitochondrial matrix
Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix; electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane
Krebs cycle on the inner mitochondrial membrane; electron transport chain in the mitochondrial matrix
questions.explanation: The Krebs cycle runs in the fluid matrix of the mitochondrion, and the electron transport chain is built into the folded inner membrane (cristae). Only glycolysis takes place in the cytosol.

questions.stem: During a sprint, a muscle cell cannot get enough oxygen. What does it produce from glucose?
options: Lactic acid and a small amount of ATP
Carbon dioxide, water and a large amount of ATP
Ethanol, carbon dioxide and a small amount of ATP
Pyruvate and oxygen and no ATP at all
questions.explanation: In anaerobic respiration human cells convert pyruvate from glycolysis into lactic acid (lactate), giving only the 2 ATP from glycolysis per glucose. Ethanol and carbon dioxide are the products in yeast.

questions.stem: Why does aerobic respiration yield far more ATP per glucose than anaerobic respiration?
options: Oxygen itself is a source of chemical energy that is stored in the ATP
Glucose is broken down completely in the mitochondria instead of stopping at lactic acid
Anaerobic respiration uses up ATP to convert pyruvate into lactic acid in the cytosol
Aerobic respiration splits each glucose into more molecules of pyruvate
questions.explanation: Without oxygen the pathway stops after glycolysis and most of the energy stays in lactic acid. With oxygen, pyruvate enters the mitochondria and is fully oxidised to carbon dioxide and water, releasing much more energy.

questions.stem: Which statement describes what oxygen does in aerobic respiration?
options: It provides the phosphate group that is added to ADP
It is the final acceptor of electrons and hydrogen, forming water
It combines with glucose in the cytosol to form two pyruvate molecules
It is converted directly into the carbon dioxide breathed out
questions.explanation: At the end of the electron transport chain oxygen accepts electrons and hydrogen ions to form water. The carbon in exhaled carbon dioxide comes from glucose, not from oxygen.

questions.stem: How does ATP supply energy for cell processes such as muscle contraction?
options: Adding a fourth phosphate to form a larger molecule releases energy
Its ribose sugar is oxidised to carbon dioxide inside the muscle fibre
It diffuses out of the cell and pulls on the filaments from outside
Breaking off its terminal phosphate to form ADP releases energy
questions.explanation: When ATP is hydrolysed to ADP and inorganic phosphate, energy is released for cellular work. Respiration then uses energy from food to rebuild ATP from ADP and phosphate.

questions.stem: A student compares two cell types. Cell P has many mitochondria with densely folded cristae; cell Q has few mitochondria. Which pairing is most likely?
options: P is a mature red blood cell; Q is a sperm cell
P is a skin surface cell; Q is a liver cell
P is a heart muscle cell; Q is a fat-storing adipose cell
P is a fat-storing adipose cell; Q is a heart muscle cell
questions.explanation: Heart muscle contracts continuously and needs a large, steady supply of ATP from aerobic respiration, so its cells are packed with mitochondria. Adipose cells are mostly a fat store with low energy demand.

questions.stem: After a hard sprint an athlete keeps breathing deeply for several minutes. Which explanation is best?
options: Extra carbon dioxide must be absorbed to rebuild the muscle cells' glucose stores
The lungs must refill with nitrogen that was used up during the sprint
Extra oxygen is needed because anaerobic respiration continues at rest
Extra oxygen is used to break down the lactic acid built up during the sprint
questions.explanation: Lactic acid built up anaerobically is later oxidised or converted back to glucose, which needs extra oxygen; this extra uptake after exercise is often called the oxygen debt. Anaerobic respiration does not continue once oxygen supply meets demand.

questions.stem: Which nutrient is the body's main and most readily used source of energy for cellular respiration?
options: Vitamins
Minerals
Carbohydrates
Proteins
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates are broken down to glucose, the main respiratory fuel. Vitamins and minerals release no usable energy but are needed for enzymes and structures.

questions.stem: Why do cells need a supply of amino acids from dietary protein?
options: To store as the body's main long-term reserve of energy
To form the phospholipid bilayer of the cell membrane
To provide the minerals needed for bone and blood
To build their own proteins, such as enzymes and membrane carriers
questions.explanation: Dietary proteins are digested to amino acids, which cells reassemble into their own proteins, including enzymes, carriers and structural proteins. The body's main long-term energy store is fat.

questions.stem: Which list gives important roles of lipids in the body?
options: Hardening bone, transmitting impulses and forming haemoglobin
Long-term energy storage, forming cell membranes and making steroid hormones
Carrying oxygen in the blood, forming enzymes and making antibodies
Forming the genetic code, building ribosomes and carrying amino acids
questions.explanation: Triglycerides store energy, phospholipids and cholesterol form membranes, and cholesterol is the starting point for steroid hormones. Carrying oxygen and forming enzymes and antibodies are jobs of proteins.

questions.stem: A person has a diet very low in iron. Which effect is most likely?
options: An enlarged thyroid because thyroxine cannot be made
Poor blood clotting because prothrombin cannot be made
Reduced haemoglobin, so less oxygen reaches cells for respiration
Weak, brittle bones because the bone matrix cannot harden
questions.explanation: Iron is part of haemoglobin, so iron deficiency causes anaemia, with less oxygen delivered and fatigue. Weak bones relate to calcium, an enlarged thyroid to iodine, and poor clotting to vitamin K.

questions.stem: Which mineral is needed to make the thyroid hormone thyroxine?
options: Iron
Calcium
Sodium
Iodine
questions.explanation: Thyroxine contains iodine, so a lack of iodine prevents the thyroid making enough hormone and can cause goitre. Iron is needed for haemoglobin.

questions.stem: Why is vitamin D important for the skeleton?
options: It increases absorption of calcium from the gut
It is the main mineral deposited in bone matrix
It forms the collagen fibres that give bone flexibility
It stimulates the red bone marrow to make platelets
questions.explanation: Vitamin D helps the intestine absorb calcium, which is then deposited in bone. Vitamin C, not D, is needed to make collagen.

questions.stem: A sailor on a long voyage with no fresh fruit or vegetables develops bleeding gums and wounds that heal poorly. Which deficiency is most likely, and why?
options: Vitamin D, needed to absorb calcium for strong teeth and bones
Vitamin K, needed by the liver to make clotting factors
Iron, needed to make haemoglobin for red blood cells
Vitamin C, needed to make the collagen in connective tissue
questions.explanation: These are signs of scurvy, caused by lack of vitamin C, which is required to make strong collagen in gums, skin and blood vessel walls. Vitamin K deficiency causes poor clotting but not the poor wound healing of scurvy.

questions.stem: Why do cells need a continuous supply of oxygen for efficient metabolism?
options: Oxygen is needed to digest food molecules into forms cells can absorb
Without oxygen enzymes cannot form their active sites in the cytosol
Without oxygen only glycolysis can supply ATP, which is far too little for most cells
Oxygen is the main raw material from which cells build their proteins and lipids
questions.explanation: Oxygen allows the aerobic stages of respiration, which supply most of a cell's ATP. Cells such as neurons depend on this and are damaged within minutes if oxygen supply stops.

questions.stem: A person eats a diet high in refined sugar and saturated fat and does little exercise. Which long-term consequence is most strongly linked to this lifestyle?
options: Increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease
Increased risk of scurvy, goitre and iron deficiency anaemia in later life
Increased risk of osteoarthritis only in the joints of the hands
Increased risk of inherited disorders such as haemophilia
questions.explanation: Excess energy intake with low activity leads to fat storage, insulin resistance and fatty deposits in arteries. Scurvy and goitre are deficiency diseases, and haemophilia is inherited, not caused by diet.

questions.stem: Which statement about vitamins is correct?
options: They are the body's main source of energy for cellular respiration
They are made in large quantities by all human body cells from glucose
They are organic substances needed in small amounts for normal metabolism
They are inorganic elements needed in large amounts for building tissues
questions.explanation: Vitamins are organic compounds needed in small amounts, often as co-enzymes; most must come from the diet. Inorganic elements such as iron and calcium are minerals.
